newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end unchanged, mkt eyes May payrolls.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end unchanged, mkt eyes May payrolls.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended largely unchanged on Thursday, as market participants opted to stay on the sidelines ahead of Friday's U.S. employment report for May.
"Bets are all placed for tomorrow," said one trader at a primary dealership. "Everyone who needed to spend has already done so."
In late trading, the 30-year bond was at 96-24/32, unchanged, while its yield stood at 6.88 percent. The two-year note was unchanged at 100-3/32 to yield 6.20 percent.
Players noted that the short end slightly outperformed the long end, with a few dealers putting on steepening trades, selling bonds for two-year notes.
The two-year to 30-year spread had widened to 71 basis points at mid-afternoon, but fell back to 68 at the close.
The market is betting that the employment report -- due Friday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT -- will be on the weak side, especially payrolls.

Nonfarm payrolls are expected to have risen 219,000 in May, according to a Reuters poll of economists -- hardly a weak number, but it represents a marked decrease from expectations of above 300,000 a week ago.
The reduced payroll forecasts stemmed from last week's benchmark revisions by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

As a result, Treasuries rallied from Friday through Tuesday, stalling on Wednesday. Players said the market tried to push higher but lack of followthrough buying prevented any rise in Treasury prices. If payrolls come in strong, players warned, the market has set itself up for a big fall, wiping out the past week's gains.
"If (the report is) not good, we could gap down very quickly," said Dave Connors, head trader at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.

But even if the report is strong, Connors and other traders do not forsee a huge correction, given improved market technicals and uncertainty whether the Federal Reserve will hike rates at its policy setting meeting in early July.
Yet, "if the unemployment rate moves (back) above five percent, there will be relief," Connors said.
Treasuries opened a bit higher, on light buying after a weak jobless claims report, which showed a 19,000 rise in the week ended May 31. The buying wasn't sustained and the early gains were erased.
Some noted that it was tough to decipher the claims data and cited inadaquete seasonals.
Treasuries drifted in narrow ranges the rest of the day amid low activity. In the absence of Retail, hedge funds and dealers controlled the day's trading.
Underpinning the market somewhat was subdued chain store sales data.
According to GovPX, volume was less than $70 billion at 1600 EDT, with most action centered in two-year, five-year and 10-year notes.
Market participants said that in addition to the payrolls and jobless rate -- seen at 5.0 percent in May -- average hourly earnings and the average workweek will garner attention on Friday morning.
Earnings are expected to have jumped 0.4 percent and the workweek is seen up slightly.
Also on Friday, wholesale inventories for April, May inflation indicators from ECRI and CIBCR, and April consumer credit are due.
The 10-year note ended at 100-2/32, up 2/32, with its yield at 6.62 percent, while the five-year note closed unchanged at 100-2/32 to yield 6.49 percent.
The three-month bill was up three basis points to 4.97 percent, the six-month bill was unchanged at 5.18 percent and the year-bill was down one basis point at 5.44 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
